text: Confidentiality means only the intended recipient can read the information
Rivest, Shamir & Adleman's 1978 example involves Alice sending information to Bob with an eavesdropper Eve
Achieving confidentiality requires information classification, secure storage, policies, training, and encryption such as the Caesar cipher
Integrity means information is whole, complete and unaltered
Changing "10 years' experience" to "2" in a CV is an example of a breach of integrity
Entering a wrong date of birth (2010 instead of 2000) is an example of a breach of integrity
Data subjects should be able to access and correct their data
Availability means information is available to authorised users when needed
The IRCTC database being down when you try to book is an example of an availability failure
Availability is achieved through reliability and redundancy and is often contracted in Service Level Agreements as "nines" such as 99.999%
100% availability has near‑infinite cost
Accountability is the concept of knowing who is responsible when something goes wrong and is supported by sign‑in logs
The McCumber Cube was proposed by John McCumber
The McCumber Cube has three dimensions, each with three values, giving 27 cells
A manager checks every cell of the McCumber Cube so no aspect is missed
One dimension of the McCumber Cube is Information states (Storage, processing, transmission)
Another dimension of the McCumber Cube is Security goals (Confidentiality, integrity, availability)
The third dimension of the McCumber Cube is Safeguards (methods) such as Policy, education, technology
An example cell of the McCumber Cube is "integrity of data during processing, ensured through education"
The security process sequence is Identification → Authentication → Authorization → Accountability
Identification creates a credible identity such as Aadhaar enrolment, ID card, roll number, employee ID, or account number
Identification is the hardest step because without identity you cannot ensure confidentiality
Authentication verifies that you are who you claim to be
Passwords are something you know for authentication
Fingerprints or biometrics are something you are/have for authentication
Multi‑factor authentication combines multiple authentication factors
Authorization is the level of access granted after authentication, based on role
Authorization requires classifying information and people and mapping them
Accountability fixes responsibility after an incident and uses logs of sign‑ins and sign‑outs
A vulnerability is a weakness such as an unlocked classroom door
An exploit uses a vulnerability to break in, such as someone walking in through an unlocked door
Not every vulnerability gets exploited
A false positive is when something genuine is flagged as malicious
A false negative is when a real attack is missed
Tighter security usually reduces efficiency, leading people to bypass security
During Thanksgiving/Christmas 2013, hackers stole customers' payment card data from Target's point‑of‑sale terminals
The attackers entered Target's network through a third‑party HVAC vendor whose access was not limited
Target's network was not segmented, allowing the vendor's access to reach the POS systems, which was an authorization failure
Malware called a RAM scraper read card data from POS memory
Data was encrypted in transmission but not in the POS RAM, creating a technical vulnerability
Target had a $1.6 million malware‑detection tool installed six months earlier
The automatic malware‑deletion feature of Target's tool was turned off and warnings were ignored because of too many false positives
Logging at Target was incomplete
Target incurred about $100 million in settlements with banks, card companies and customers
Target faced more than 90 lawsuits after the breach
Target's holiday‑season profit fell 46 % after the breach
The breach caused intangible losses such as loss of goodwill, customer trust and reputation
The Target breach was a watershed moment for US cybersecurity regulation
Investing in technology alone is insufficient if management processes fail, as employees can circumvent security
Andrew Grove's book "Only the Paranoid Survive" argues that a paranoid mindset suits cybersecurity
Some firms choose to invest the bare minimum and pay fines because $100 M is tiny compared to $72 B revenue
Whitman & Mattord list critical characteristics of information as availability, accuracy, authenticity, confidentiality, integrity, utility, and possession
Components of an information system are software, hardware, data, people, procedures, and networks
Good access‑control practice includes role‑based permissions, periodic review and revocation of rights, and audited access logs
An SQL‑injectable input field before any attack is a vulnerability
The crafted SQL string that uses a vulnerable field is an exploit
A safe app quarantined as malware is a false positive
Malware that slips through detection is a false negative
GRC stands for Governance, Risk and Compliance
Three approaches to GRC are a GRC framework, standards‑driven (ISO/NIST), and a textbook organisational‑planning approach
COBIT is a GRC framework from ISACA and the IT community
COSO is a GRC framework used for accounting and internal control
COSO ERM is a GRC framework for enterprise risk
BS 7799 evolved into ISO/IEC 17799 and then ISO/IEC 27001, which follows the PDCA cycle
NIST is the open, free US alternative to ISO standards
Controls can be preventive, detective or corrective
iPremier experienced a DDoS attack while having no plans, no logs and a weak hosting partner
Breaches are increasing and the Marriott 2019 breach involved about 500 million records
Louis Pasteur said "Fortune favours the prepared mind"
The standards-driven approach treats cyber security separately by implementing a standard from ISO or NIST
The standards-driven approach suits small and mid-size firms and can also be used within a GRC framework
The textbook (organisational planning) approach makes cyber security a priority in strategic planning together with contingency planning
Following the 2016 debit-card breach, the RBI made cyber security a strategic function in banks, separate from IT, and required chip cards
Governance is positioned higher than management
The board establishes management and then evaluates, directs, and monitors it
Linking cyber security to governance makes cyber security a strategic priority
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act was enacted after accounting scandals such as Enron
COBIT was created by ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association)
COBIT stands for Control Objectives for Information and related Technology
The current version discussed is COBIT 5
COBIT principles include meeting stakeholder needs, covering the enterprise end to end, a single integrated framework, a holistic approach, and separating governance from management
COBIT's management cycle consists of Plan (APO), Build (BAI), Run (DSS), Monitor (MEA), and governance activities are Evaluate, Direct, Monitor
COSO stands for Committee of Sponsoring Organizations, an accounting community credited to the American Accounting Association
In COSO ERM, risk response closes the loop
Internal controls protect assets, maintain records, provide accurate information, prepare financial reports, improve efficiency, encourage policy adherence, and ensure legal compliance
Types of control include preventive (deter problems), detective (find problems), and corrective (fix after detection)
ISO/IEC 27001 is the basic standard written in the PDCA cycle for continual improvement
ISO/IEC 27002 is the code of practice
The ISO/IEC 27000 series includes over 50 standards covering verticals and horizontals

The company is one of the top two sellers, rivaled by MarketTop
The company's competitive edge is customer experience
The company conducts quarterly performance reviews

Jack Samuelson is the CEO of the company

Motives for DDoS attacks include hacktivism, cyber vandalism, cyber warfare, extortion and rivalry

A hot, warm or cold standby site should have existed for the company
A de facto standard is widely adopted without a formal standards body
A de jure standard is formally approved by a standards body
Guidelines are non‑mandatory recommendations
Business Continuity (BCP) is led by the CIO for severe incidents requiring relocation to an alternate site
An incident is an attack that actually happened by exploiting a vulnerability
A threat is something that could happen
The analogy compares shoe soles giving grip to the possibility of slipping on a banana peel in the rain
Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) is the total outage the process owner will accept
Owners often say zero downtime, but zero has an enormous cost
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the time to bring the system back live
Work Recovery Time (WRT) is the time after the system is live until work actually resumes
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the point in time to which data can be recovered
Hourly backups give an RPO of one hour
MTD equals RTO plus WRT
FIPS 199 can be used to rate impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability as low, moderate or high
The shorter the desired downtime, the higher the cost of recovery
The longer the downtime, the higher the cost of disruption
The optimum downtime is where the cost curves of recovery and disruption cross
Contingency planning is described as a negotiation for time
Incident response is organized before, during, and after an incident
Every incident should be documented with what, when, where, why and how
An after-action review should be held after an incident
Incident indicators are possible, probable, and definite
Under GDPR a breach must be reported within 72 hours

A warm site is ready within a defined time
A cold site provides basic space and takes the longest to activate
Testing of contingency plans includes drills and simulated attacks
Carnegie Mellon’s incident response plan is an example of a detailed plan

text: A cyber security policy must never conflict with the law
Policy maps to standards, which map to procedures and guidelines
The three levels of security policy are EISP, ISSP, and SysSP
SETA stands for Security Education, Training and Awareness
Bochman describes "cyber insecurity" and recommends protecting crown jewels by reducing digital pathways
A regulation is a policy that is enforceable in law
A policy applies to everyone for the collective good and fairness
India's IT industry grew after policy changes such as software technology parks and the 1991 liberalisation
A badly framed policy, for example a prohibition on internet access, leads to violations
The terms of reference for Justice B.N. Srikrishna's committee are to protect privacy without inhibiting the potential of digital technologies
A good policy should never conflict with the law and must stand up in court
A good policy must be properly supported and administered, such as implementing a firewall that actually blocks illegal sites
A good policy should contribute to the success of the organisation
A good policy should involve end users in its formulation
Arthur Andersen adopted a document‑retention policy to keep documents "while relevant" and then shredded audit evidence
Courts saw Arthur Andersen's shredding of audit evidence as destruction of evidence and a policy in conflict with the law
Retention rules today use specific periods, for example IITM keeps answer scripts about four years
If an employee accesses child pornography at work, the organisation can defend itself only if it has a clear policy prohibiting illegal sites and enforces it with a firewall
A policy is broad, abstract, strategic, long‑term and rarely changed
Standards are more detailed statements of how a policy is implemented
When breach reporting changes from 72 to 24 hours, the standard should be updated, not the policy
Procedures and guidelines provide step‑by‑step implementation, such as firewall configuration rules
Policy must be disseminated to employees, for example through the Tata Code of Conduct
An Enterprise Information Security Policy (EISP) sets strategic direction, scope and tone, and assigns responsibilities
An EISP contains a statement of purpose, definitions of information security elements, need for security, roles and responsibilities, and references to standards such as NIST or ISO
An EISP may include a rule that employees will be given email to be used per procedures
An Issue‑Specific Security Policy (ISSP) provides detailed, targeted guidance on using a technology or resource such as email, web, viruses, hacking tools, work from home, or BYOD
An ISSP also indemnifies the organisation against liability
An ISSP may prohibit personal use of official email and set storage space limits
A System‑Specific Security Policy (SysSP) operates at the implementation level and includes managerial guidance and technical specifications such as access control lists and configuration rules
A mail server can be configured with a 5 GB quota as part of a SysSP
Indemnify means to absolve of responsibility
Hospitals indemnify doctors and an ISSP protects the organisation when an employee misuses resources

An access control list maps users or roles to resources they can access and defines permitted actions such as read, write, create, modify, delete, compare, copy, and also specifies when, where and how access is allowed
Windows XP includes roles such as administrators, backup operators, guests, and power users
Configuration rules include firewall rules that specify which sites or IPs are allowed
Configuration rules also include IDS rules
A firewall prevents access and is preventive
An IDS only detects and raises an alarm

INL recommends identifying the most critical functions (“crown jewels”), mapping the digital terrain, cutting digital pathways, adding analog/manual backups and redundancy, and using air gaps.
The CCE (Consequence-driven Cyber-informed Engineering) process has four phases: consequence prioritisation, system‑of‑systems analysis, consequence‑based targeting, and mitigations and protections.
CCE is aimed at nation‑state‑level threats.
CIE (Cyber‑Informed Engineering) builds cybersecurity into the concept and design stage and treats cyber attack as another failure mode.

Whitman's definitions: standards are detailed mandatory statements; guidelines are non‑mandatory recommendations; procedures are step‑by‑step instructions; practices are examples of actions that show compliance.
EISP sections include a statement of purpose, information security elements, need for security, roles and responsibilities, and reference to other standards.
"Authorized access and usage of equipment" is an ISSP section, not an EISP section.
For a policy to be enforceable it must be disseminated, readable, understood, agreed to, and uniformly enforced.
ISSPS can be managed as independent documents, a single comprehensive document, or a modular document.
SysSPs can be developed with or before ISSPs.
Managerial guidance SysSPs state management's intent from a business view; technical specification SysSPs are the ACLs and configuration rules.
A capability table lists what each user can access; an ACL lists who can access each asset.
Configuration rules govern how a security system reacts to data it receives.
Cyber hygiene refers to routine practices for digital health, while cybersecurity is the broader strategy.
Risk management is proactive and its unit of analysis is the asset.
Risk management consists of three phases: identification, assessment, and control.
The goal of risk management is to reduce risk, not to eliminate it.
Residual risk is the risk that remains after current protections are applied.
Risk is calculated as loss frequency times loss magnitude minus the percentage mitigated by current controls plus measurement uncertainty.
Attack surface (attack vector) is a two‑dimensional picture with threats on one axis and assets on the other.
Equifax's 2017 breach has been charted using the attack surface model.
Residual risk remains after base protection, extra safeguards, and closing vulnerabilities.
Risk assessment determines loss frequency, evaluates loss magnitude, calculates risk, and assesses risk acceptability.
Risk control selects a strategy, justifies it with cost‑benefit analysis, implements it, and monitors it continuously.
Assets are categorised into six types: people, procedures, data, software, hardware, and networking.
Each asset is assigned a tag or ID with attributes such as name, IP address, MAC address, type, serial number, manufacturer, version, location, and owner.
People assets receive a security clearance level, and data assets receive attributes like owner, creator, size, storage location, online/offline status, and backup status.
Data classification levels for a business include public, for official use only, sensitive, and classified.
The US military data classification levels are unclassified, sensitive but unclassified, confidential, secret, and top secret.
Asset value is based on business impact rather than purchase price.
Weighted factor analysis scores each asset against criteria such as impact on revenue, profitability, and public image to produce a score out of 100.
A customer order via SSL was scored 100 because without it the business would stop.

Asset valuation is done internally

text: An operating system is the interface between the human and the hardware for input, output, and compute
All battles are fought in the applications and operating system space
Kernel space and user space are distinct areas in an operating system
Protection rings are a hierarchy of privileges in an operating system, with Ring 0 being the most privileged and providing full hardware control
Rings 1–3 are restricted privilege levels typically used for user programs, with Ring 3 being the usual level for user programs
Attackers seek kernel‑level privilege so they can act as the watchman
Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption
A problem with symmetric encryption is how to share the key safely
If a symmetric key is captured later, every past message encrypted with that key can be decrypted
The cracking of Germany's Enigma helped the Allies win WWII
Public‑key (asymmetric) encryption encrypts with the recipient's public key and only the recipient's private key can decrypt
Hash functions are one‑way functions that produce a fixed‑length output for any input
Changing a single bit of input to a hash function causes the entire hash output to change
Hash functions are used to check integrity, such as the MD5 value shown next to a download
Hash functions are used in forensics
The OSI model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, and application
A port identifies a process with a network connection
TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery with acknowledgements, is slower, and is used for files
UDP provides fast delivery with no guarantees and is used for streaming, audio and video calls
Network access control technologies such as LDAP, Kerberos, and RADIUS identify every user on a network
A firewall is a security guard at the network's entry and exit enforcing rules
Firewalls at higher OSI layers inspect more and cost more
A DMZ (demilitarised zone) is a buffer zone between the internet and the internal network, reached through a proxy
Unpatched routers and firewalls are described as "cracks in the wall"
A VPN (virtual private network) creates an encrypted tunnel over the internet that makes a remote user part of the office network
For a hacker a VPN is the "key to the kingdom"
A group is only as strong as its weakest member
The cyber kill chain consists of Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command & Control, and Actions on objectives
The cyber kill chain is compared to a commando raid involving reconnaissance, choosing weapons, getting in, staying in, and reporting back
Untargeted attacks use mass emails and spread through anyone who clicks
Targeted attacks, such as espionage, focus on a specific victim, are more expensive, and carry higher risk of exposure
A vulnerability is the weak point or thinnest spot of a bunker
An exploit is the weaponised means to break through a vulnerability
A payload is what does the damage once inside and is the deadliest part that antivirus primarily looks for
A Word macro vulnerability can be an exploit that downloads code, whose payload installs a RAT
Malware is a general term for malicious software
A Trojan is malware that gives the attacker a back door and can also deliver ransomware
RAT stands for remote administration tool; legitimate examples include TeamViewer and malicious ones are sold on the dark web with subscriptions
